The Rufous rat-kangaroo Aepyprymnus rufescens is a moderately sized potoroid exhibiting a suite of life-history traits characteristic of a slow-paced reproductive strategy. Neonates emerge after a brief gestation period of approximately 23 days [tg = approximately 23 days] when maintained at an ambient temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], a remarkably short developmental interval for a mammal of this body mass. At parturition, the newborn young, or joey, weighs merely 0.1 grams [Wwb = 0.1 grams], an altricial state typical of macropodoid marsupials. This minuscule neonate, born after a period of internal fertilisation and rapid embryogenesis, then undertakes a prolonged period of development within the maternal pouch. The ultimate adult body mass attained by this species is approximately 3250 grams [Wwi = approximately 3250 grams], placing it among the larger members of the Potoroidae family. This substantial size difference between the newborn and the fully grown adult underscores the immense energetic investment required during lactation and pouch life.

Reproductive output in Aepyprymnus rufescens is notably constrained, with females typically producing three litters per year [F_R_i = three litters per year] under the optimal thermal conditions of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This rate represents the maximum recorded reproductive frequency for the species. The dependent joey remains permanently attached to the teat for the first several months of life, undergoing a sustained period of nursing and growth before it is ready to begin the transition to independence. When the young rat-kangaroo finally vacates the pouch permanently, it does so at a weaning age of 162 days after birth [tx = 162 days after birth] and at a body mass of approximately 950 grams [Wwx = approximately 950 grams] at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This weaning mass represents roughly 29 percent of the ultimate adult weight, indicating that significant somatic growth is still required after nutritional emancipation from the mother. The period of maternal dependency is thus both metabolically costly and temporally extended.

Sexual maturation in this species exhibits a pronounced sexual dimorphism in timing, a pattern observed across many polygynous or promiscuous macropodoids. Under stable environmental conditions, specifically at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], female individuals reach puberty at 333 days after birth [tp = 333 days after birth]. In contrast, males attain reproductive maturity considerably earlier, achieving puberty at 280 days after birth [tp = 280 days after birth] at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This divergence suggests that males may begin producing viable gametes and exhibiting reproductive behaviours while still completing their own somatic growth, a strategy that can be advantageous when scramble competition for oestrous females is intense. The onset of gametogenesis and testicular descent in the male therefore precedes the full development of skeletal and muscular mass, a life-history trade-off that aligns with field observations of younger males actively pursuing copulation opportunities. The age at first successful reproduction for both sexes likely occurs somewhat later than these pubertal milestones due to social and competitive constraints.

Basal metabolic rate in the Rufous rat-kangaroo was assessed via respirometry on captive animals. At a thermoneutral temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], the maximum resting oxygen consumption was recorded at 1069 milliliters per hour [JOi = 1069 milliliters per hour] for an individual with a wet body mass of 2820 grams. This metabolic rate, expressed relative to body size, is consistent with values reported for other potoroids and reflects the relatively low mass-specific metabolic demands of a hindgut-fermenting herbivore inhabiting the subtropical forests of eastern Australia. The measurement underscores the energetic baseline required for tissue upkeep and basal maintenance requirements under thermoneutral conditions. Such data are crucial for parameterising the daily energetic costs of tissue upkeep and for understanding the metabolic constraints acting on the species' overall life-history pace, particularly the extended gestational and lactational periods. It also provides a physiological anchor for understanding how the animal allocates resources towards activity, thermoregulation, and reproduction in its natural habitat.

Maximum lifespan in the Rufous rat-kangaroo is considerable for a mammal of its size, with the oldest documented individuals reaching approximately 4672 days [am = approximately 4672 days] when kept under controlled captive conditions at an ambient temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. Such longevity, combined with a delayed maturation and low annual reproductive output, aligns with a demographic strategy oriented toward adult survival rather than high fecundity. The species is therefore vulnerable to population declines if adult mortality increases due to habitat fragmentation or predation by introduced carnivores. The combination of a short gestation, a long pouch life with a relatively high weaning mass, and a late age at first reproduction in females underscores the profound maternal investment per surviving offspring. This suite of life-history traits makes Aepyprymnus rufescens a classic example of a K-selected marsupial in a perennially uncertain environment.
